article_title: Considering Literacy Coaching Responsibilities in Terms of Teacher Change
title: Level 3 sustaining efforts: extend coach learning and foster independent teacher learning communities
description: At the third level, mentoring turns inward: coaches attend district, regional, and national professional development to deepen literacy knowledge and support sustaining efforts. Advocacy shifts to helping teacher groups "support each other in their effort to improve instructional skills as independent learning communities." Michelle's monthly all-district coaching meetings and Diane's facilitation of a reciprocal teaching group that begins meeting independently illustrate this level.
citation: Smith, A. T. (2009). Considering Literacy Coaching Responsibilities in Terms of Teacher Change. University of Washington Bothell. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED530353

article_title: The Case against Conditional Argumentation.
title: Debate as a laboratory for argumentation theory, contingent on keeping debate practices accountable to argumentation principles
description: This pattern holds that academic debate can serve as a laboratory for studying argumentation theory — for example, testing standards for assessing arguments and decision-making — but only if debate practices remain accountable to argumentation principles. Herbeck notes that despite extensive competition, few insights into argumentation theory have resulted, and cites Goodnight's observation that "a significant gap seems to be developing between theories of argument and theories of debate." Permitting conditional arguments, he argues, turns debate into "a laboratory for perfecting itself" and severs debate from argumentation theory.
citation: Herbeck. (1990). The Case against Conditional Argumentation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED322540

article_title: The Effectiveness of "Direct Instruction" on Reading Achievement.
title: Direct Instruction's distinctive teaching practices: scripted presentation, small groups, unison responding, signals, pacing, correction procedures, and oral reading
description: According to the article, Watkins (1988) identified the practices that distinguish Direct Instruction from more traditional approaches. The article lists them as "scripted presentation, small groups,unisonresponding,signals,pacing,correction procedures and oral reading." These lesson-level routines structure how teachers present material, how students respond, and how errors are corrected during instruction.
citation: Mosley, Allen M. (1997). The Effectiveness of "Direct Instruction" on Reading Achievement. ERIC Document ED402553. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED402553

article_title: Developing the Level of Adoption Survey to Inform Collaborative Discussion regarding Educational Innovation
title: Continually culling, clustering, and redefining the technology catalogue to track converging emergent technologies
description: The LoA instrument's technology list is treated as an evolving artifact: the authors report "continually culling, refining, redefining and clustering our list of technologies" to represent current emergent yet applicable instructional technologies. They created a single classroom video category spanning delivery formats, added mobile devices, separated wikis/blogging from social networking, identified virtual worlds as a singular category, and removed production and laboratory software increasingly seen as standard tools.
citation: Orr, D., & Mrazek, R. (2009). Developing the level of adoption survey to inform collaborative discussion regarding educational innovation. Canadian Journal of Learning and Technology, V35(2). https://www.cjlt.ca

article_title: Using the "Language Inquiry" as a Teaching Device.
title: Expert-panel item selection: statements drawn from real settings, winnowed by linguist votes to consensus items
description: The Inquiry's items were not invented: the attitudes tested were heard in methods classes, conventions, workshops, and printed sources such as newspaper editorials. Ten linguists first responded to 150 statements, then voted on 135 statements using Agree, Moderately agree, No opinion, and Disagree; the author generally kept items where at least seven out of ten linguists concurred, yielding 109 such items, of which 97 were used, with three added where Agree and Moderately agree totaled nine or ten for content balance.
citation: Frogner, Ellen A. (1969). Using the Language Inquiry as a Teaching Device. Illinois State-Wide Curriculum Study Center in the Preparation of Secondary English Teachers (ISCPET). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED034768

article_title: On the Influence on Learning of Student Compliance with Prompts Fostering Self-Regulated Learning
title: Two-category taxonomy of SRL prompts by how compliance can be evaluated: explicit vs inferred compliance prompts
description: The article classifies MetaTutor's SRL prompts into two categories based on how compliance can be evaluated. "Explicit compliance prompts" are those for which compliance "can be explicitly assessed from students subsequent responses", e.g. prompts requiring a yes/no answer or a specific action within a time frame. "Inferred compliance prompts" are those for which "compliance needs to be inferred by mining a variety of behaviors", such as staying on or moving from a page. The article mines window length, number of fixations, and number of SRL strategies to evaluate the latter.
citation: Lallé, S., Mudrick, N., Conati, C., Taub, M., Azevedo, R. (2017). On the Influence on Learning of Student Compliance with Prompts Fostering Self-Regulated Learning. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2017/

article_title: Children's Problem-Solving in Serious Games: The "Fine-Tuning System (FTS)" Elaborated
title: Three fading-based scaffolding approaches: supportive, intrinsic and reflective scaffolding
description: The paper enumerates three scaffolding approaches based on fading, drawn from Jackson et al. (1998). "As supportive scaffolding fades, the task is the same as it was before, but the goal is for the learner to have internalized the procedures and concepts which had been scaffolded". In intrinsic scaffolding the task changes as the scaffold fades, gradually introducing underlying complexity. Reflective scaffolding makes reflection explicit by eliciting articulation, for example player-character conversation with an NPC, faded by gradually disabling conversations from most to least helpful.
citation: Obikwelu, C, Read, J, and Sim, G. (2013). Children’s Problem-Solving in Serious Games: The “Fine-Tuning System (FTS)” Elaborated. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning Volume 11 Issue 1. https://www.ejel.org

article_title: The Evaluation Toolkit: A Work-in-Progress.
title: Five core areas of classroom technology use as organizing units for assessment
description: The Toolkit structures its materials around five recurring forms of student work with technology. As printed, "The Toolkit currently focuses on five core areas of technology use commonly encountered in classrooms": Internet Research, Data Collection and Representation (spreadsheets and graphing tools), Live Presentations, Web Design, and Illustrated Reports. Each area receives its own affordance analysis, conceptual framework, and checklist entries, so teachers can locate assessment guidance by the kind of digital product students produce.
citation: The Evaluation Toolkit: A Work-in-Progress. (2002). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED463744

article_title: Implicit scaffolding in interactive simulations: Design strategies to support multiple educational goals
title: Four-category design pattern for implicit scaffolding in simulations
description: The article organizes implicit scaffolding strategies into four categories that work together: scaffolding the general concept (scope, sequence, interactivity), scaffolding students' framing of sim use (opening screen, initial interaction), scaffolding to enable sense making (representations, feedback, layout, range of interactions, illuminating cases), and scaffolding for continued engagement (puzzles and challenges). The authors state: "We divide our description of implicit scaffolding strategies into four categories: Scaffolding 1) the general concept, 2) students’ framing of sim use, 3) to enable sense making, and 4) for continued engagement." Together these enable agency while affording
citation: Podolefsky, N. S., Moore, E. B., & Perkins, K. K. (2013). Implicit scaffolding in interactive simulations: Design strategies to support multiple educational goals. http://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulation/energy-skate-park-basics

article_title: Using Situational Leadership To Reach the Whole Population.
title: Four-quadrant progression from unready learner to independent library user with matching instructor behavior
description: The paper organizes library learners into four developmental quadrants, each calling for a different instructor stance. Quadrant one students are unready and unable and receive high support and high direction, often more telling than teaching; quadrant two students, the "average freshman", receive high direction and support with more teaching and critical-thinking assignments; quadrant three students receive low direction and medium support as the librarian shifts to consultant; quadrant four independent users receive low direction and support, mainly through signage. The charted pattern pairs student characteristics with supportive instructor behavior at each level.
citation: Carder, Linda; Pracht, Carl; Willingham, J. Robert. (1996). Using Situational Leadership to Reach the Whole Population. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED406998

article_title: Cognitive Apprenticeship and Instructional Technology. Technical Report.
title: Four methods of reflection on performance: imitation, replay, abstracted replay, and spatial reification
description: The paper enumerates four ways of permitting students to reflect on their performance: "(1) imitation, (2) replay, (3) abstracted replay and (4) spatial reification," illustrated via tennis coaching. Technology makes the last three forms possible, which the authors call "a genuinely new teaching method emerging out of technology." Reflection turns the student's performance into an object of study, lets students compare their performance to others', supports characterizing strategies abstractly, and permits comparison of multiple performances to form abstractions about expert versus novice performance.
citation: Collins, Allan. (1988). Cognitive Apprenticeship and Instructional Technology. Technical Report. BBN Report No. 6899, BBN Labs, Inc. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED331465

article_title: Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Language Proficiency Acquisition, Assessment, and Communicative Behavior, Series B. Student Edition. Bilingual Education Teacher Training Packets.
title: Functional Approach progression from oral dialogue (BICS) to written discourse (CALP)
description: Larsen-Pusey's Functional Approach is a teaching model that bridges the gap between oral skills and academic language: "This model focuses on taking the students from BICS(oral dialogue) to *6ALP (written discourse)". It moves students from context-embedded to context-reduced situations and from cognitively undemanding to cognitively demanding tasks, drawing on generative linguistics, psycholinguistics, sociolinguistics, and educational psychology. The packet's model diagram sequences dialogue plays and skits, reported speech, reader's theater, narrative and expository reading, and note-taking, dialog journals, and written reports, with activities (e.g., Activity III's five steps from dialog
citation: Calderon, Margarita; And Others. (1982). Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Language Proficiency Acquisition, Assessment, and Communicative Behavior, Series B. Student Edition. Bilingual Education Teacher Training Packets. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED226607

article_title: Funds of Knowledge: Learning from Language Minority Households. ERIC Digest.
title: Funds of Knowledge Teacher-Research Model (Tucson Project)
description: A research model, described in the digest, in which teachers and university researchers in education and anthropology "enter minority households and discover knowledge and other resources therein" and then build classroom practice from what they find. It had three components: an ethnographic community study of household funds of knowledge, after-school teacher labs, and classroom studies implementing innovations based on the household study.
citation: Funds of Knowledge: Learning from Language Minority Households. ERIC Digest. (1994). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED367146

article_title: Social Sciences Education Framework for California Public Schools, Kindergarten and Grades One through Twelve.
title: Grade-span structure of program goals with illustrative, non-sequential level objectives
description: The framework organizes objectives across four grade spans—K-3, 4-6, 7-8, and 9-12—stating program goals for the whole span and illustrative level objectives for each. It explains that 'Illustrative level objectives are presented for each of the grade spans. These objectives are not comprehensive as to objectives that might be specified for any particular program goal, nor are they sequential. They are, however, responsive to the changing maturity of students.' Districts are responsible for further delineation into behavioral objectives.
citation: Social Sciences Education Framework for California Public Schools, Kindergarten and Grades One through Twelve. (1975). California State Department of Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED120079

article_title: Literacy Coaching: Engaging and Learning with Teachers
title: Ground coaching conversations in the work of children
description: A recurring coaching pattern: conversations about instruction start from authentic artifacts of student learning such as written responses, writing samples, and actual Running Records. The author invites teachers to question when children were most and least engaged and to examine prompts, re-reading, self-correction, and privileged strategies. Looking across artifacts, teachers decided to broaden the range of written responses students completed after reading. These instructional conversations around children's work, the author writes, "challenged us to envision multiple possibilities."
citation: Dozier, C. L. (2008). Literacy coaching: Engaging and learning with teachers. The Language and Literacy Spectrum, 18. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1059644

article_title: Guided Inquiry into a Physics Equation
title: Guided Equation Appropriation
description: When a student encounters a physics equation directly (e.g., looked up or given), they can often derive or apply it long before they understand what it means or implies. This pattern sequences instruction to build understanding in the other direction: mechanistic, intuitive reasoning first, formal equation second, deep interpretive reading of the equation third — with a mentor making seven specific kinds of moves throughout to keep the student's own reasoning central rather than substituting the mentor's expertise for it.
citation: Kapon, S., & Schvartzer, M. (2024). Guided Inquiry into a Physics Equation. *Cognition and Instruction, 42*(1), 159-206. [https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2023.2197232](https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2023.2197232)

article_title: Zone of Proximal Development and the World of the Child.
title: Guided participation: five components of adult-child learning activity
description: Drawing on Rogoff (1990), the paper describes guided participation as "a process during which the adult and child determine and carry out the learning activity" in real world activities. It enumerates five components: selecting the activity in which guidance takes place; deciding the goals of the activity; establishing bridges between what the child knows and what the adult wants to induct the child into; ensuring that the child attains independent functioning; and communicating in a number of dimensions. The pattern characterises how adults structure joint activity so children are inducted into culture by more competent members.
citation: Seng, Seok-Hoon. (1997). Zone of Proximal Development and the World of the Child. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED416957

article_title: Guiding Teacher Learning: Insider Studies of Classroom-Based Work with Teachers. Craft Paper 94-1.
title: Guided practice serves four broad, overlapping purposes for teacher learning
description: In their reading of the literature, the authors found that guided practice may serve four broad and overlapping purposes: "They include helping teachers (1) realize visions of teaching in their daily practice; (2) implement a new curriculum or teaching strategies; (3) study their practice in systematic ways; and (4) restructure teaching." Beyond these orienting purposes, guides also pursue emergent, immediate goals arising from practical realities and the teacher's concerns. The purposes a guide pursues interact with the participants' relationship and the context.
citation: Feiman-Nemser, Sharon, et al. (1994). Guiding Teacher Learning: Insider Studies of Classroom-Based Work with Teachers. Craft Paper 94-1. National Center for Research on Teacher Learning. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED377169

article_title: Educational Psychology, Unit 5: Facilitating Complex Thinking (Arduini-Van Hoose, 2020)
title: Hunter's Effective Teaching Model
description: Madeline Hunter combined a number of direct-instruction techniques into a single, comprehensive approach she called **mastery teaching** (distinct from the separate term "mastery learning") or the **effective teaching model** (M. Hunter, 1982; R. Hunter, 2004). Its features span before, during, and after a lesson. **Before the lesson**, the curriculum is analyzed into its basic elements and how they relate to each other, expressed at a level appropriate to the students (e.g., teaching photosynthesis to advanced students as chemical reactions involving chlorophyll and carbon dioxide, versus to first-graders as a process akin to breathing). **Preparing students to learn** makes the most of the
citation: Hunter, M. (1982). *Mastery teaching*. TIP Publications.

article_title: The Iowa Guide for Curriculum Improvement in Industrial Arts, K-12. A Study of Industrial Technology.
title: Industrial arts pyramid program across operational levels
description: The guide recommends a pyramid program structure (Figure 4) in which elementary level activities introduce industrial technology in the world of work with emphasis on self-concepts, insights, and awareness; junior high core courses provide comprehensive exploration of industrial-technological clusters; and senior high cluster specialization courses enable exploration in depth and beginning specialization. The pyramid concept is "aimed at helping all students to become familiar with the values of an industrial-technological society, to integrate these values into their personal value system, and to implement these values."
citation: The Iowa Guide for Curriculum Improvement in Industrial Arts, K-12. A Study of Industrial Technology. (1975). Iowa State Dept. of Public Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED113517

article_title: Curiosity to Question: Tracing productive engagement in an interdisciplinary course-based research experience
title: Interdisciplinary Course-Based Research Experience
description: A Course-Based Research Experience (CBRE) has a whole class work on authentic, open research instead of individually supervised capstone projects. This pattern adapts CBRE for interdisciplinary contexts by deliberately recruiting students across disciplines and levels (undergraduate and graduate together) and organizing the course around a **shared scientific paper as a boundary object** that different students engage differently depending on their own discipline, while the class collectively builds a shared understanding of what counts as a strong research paper across disciplines. It extends [Productive Disciplinary Engagement](../principles/inquiry-based-learning.md) (Engle & Conant's fou
citation: Papendieck, A., & Clarke, J. A. (2024). Curiosity to Question: Tracing productive engagement in an interdisciplinary course-based research experience. *Journal of the Learning Sciences, 33*(2), 323-364. [https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2347597](https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2347597)

article_title: IUPUI's HIP Taxonomy for ePortfolio: A Tool for Development, Implementation, and Scaling. Occasional Paper No. 57
title: IUPUI ePortfolio HIP taxonomy: four attributes of high-impact ePortfolio practice at three ascending levels of impact
description: The taxonomy identifies four attributes of high-impact ePortfolio practice: "1. ePortfolio is central to the curricular design of the course, program, or university experience. 2. ePortfolio pedagogies support integrative, self-directed learning, and student identity development. 3. ePortfolio making skills are explicitly taught to students. 4. ePortfolio assessment is holistic and aligned with learning processes and outcomes." Each attribute is described along three levels of impact—high, higher, and highest—with each level incorporating all characteristics of previous levels. Impact increases as adoption scales from a single course to course sequences, degree programs, and the whole underg
citation: Kahn, S., Freeman, T., & Powell, A. A. (2021, November). IUPUI's HIP taxonomy for ePortfolio: A tool for development, implementation, and scaling (Occasional Paper No. 57). Urbana, IL: University of Illinois and Indiana University, National Institute for Learning Outcomes Assessment (NILOA). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED619086

article_title: Unit 8: Instruction (Educational Psychology, Arduini-Van Hoose)
title: Just-In-Time Teaching (JiTT)
description: Just-In-Time Teaching (JiTT), developed by Gregor Novak and colleagues (Novak et al., 1999), relies on a feedback loop between web-based pre-class materials and the classroom. Students prepare by reading assigned material and completing short web-based assignments; their responses reach the instructor a few hours before class, letting the instructor adapt that day's lesson to exactly what students are struggling with. This shifts class time from content transfer toward active learning and cooperative problem-solving. Three types of JiTT activities serve different moments in the learning cycle: **WarmUps** are short, pre-instruction assignments that prompt initial thinking about upcoming cont
citation: Novak, G. M., Patterson, E. T., Gavrin, A. D., & Christian, W. (1999). *Just-in-time teaching: Blending active learning with web technology*. Prentice Hall.

article_title: The Iowa Guide for Curriculum Improvement in Industrial Arts, K-12. A Study of Industrial Technology.
title: Level-differentiated emphases: awareness, exploration, specialization
description: The guide differentiates the function of industrial arts by school level: elementary school provides INSIGHTS into and AWARENESS of the industrial-technical society; junior high courses provide EXPLORATION of the adult world of work and support of SELF CONCEPTS during early adolescence; senior high provides concentrated, specialized study with career EXPLORATION IN DEPTH and BEGINNING SPECIALIZATION. Operational level goals and expected outcomes are listed for each level under career emphasis and industrial-technological emphasis headings.
citation: The Iowa Guide for Curriculum Improvement in Industrial Arts, K-12. A Study of Industrial Technology. (1975). Iowa State Dept. of Public Instruction. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED113517

article_title: Reading Alone Together: Enhancing Extensive Reading via Student-Student Cooperation in Second Language Instruction.
title: Literature Circles with rotating collaborative-skill roles for small-group pleasure reading
description: Midway between whole-class and individual reading, Literature Circles have "L2 students read for pleasure in small, self-selected groups that meet regularly to discuss books that the members themselves have chosen." The article recommends enhancing discussions with instruction in collaborative skills via rotating roles: Paraphraser, Praiser, Controversy kindler, and Connector, with teachers supplying role gambits such as "Have you ever thought about it this way?" Roles rotate so everyone practices the skills.
citation: Jacobs, George M. (2000). Reading Alone Together: Enhancing Extensive Reading via Student-Student Cooperation in Second Language Instruction. Paper presented at the Malaysian International Conference on English Language Teaching, Malacca, Malaysia. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED444377

article_title: What Teacher Education Students Learn about Collaboration from Problem-Based Learning
title: Seven-step Maastricht PBL tutorial cycle with progressive case disclosure and group presentation
description: The course used a hybrid form of the 7-step Maastricht PBL model in which a case 'story' unfolds progressively over tutorials through 'pages' of information following a trigger scenario. Table 1 structures the cycle: whole-class work on clarification, definition, analysis and review; small groups establishing learning goals; self-directed study; reconvening to report and synthesise; a non-contact preparation week; a 15-minute group presentation with anonymous peer and tutor feedback; and a post-presentation debrief with self-assessment against a four-dimension tutorial performance survey.
citation: Murray-Harvey, R., Pourshafie, T., & Santos Reyes, W. (2013). What teacher education students learn about collaboration from problem-based learning. Journal of Problem Based Learning in Higher Education, 1(1), 114-134. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1108330

article_title: A New Framework for Teaching in the Cognitive Domain. ERIC Digest.
title: Demonstration, application, and integration corollaries of Merrill's framework
description: The digest enumerates the supporting generalizations for Merrill's remaining phases. Demonstration requires showing rather than merely telling, with demonstrations consistent with the learning goal, appropriate learner guidance, and relevant media that do not compete for attention. Application requires practice consistent with objectives, coaching that is gradually withdrawn, and a sequence of varied problems. Integration holds that "Learning is promoted when learners are encouraged to integrate (transfer) the new knowledge or skill into their everyday life", with corollaries of public demonstration, reflection, and creation.
citation: Molenda, Michael. (2002). A New Framework for Teaching in the Cognitive Domain. ERIC Digest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED470983

article_title: A Brief Introduction to Cooperative Learning.
title: Nine key elements structuring a cooperative lesson
description: The chapter enumerates the key elements of a cooperative lesson: positive interdependence (with goal, resource, reward, identity, role, and outside enemy variants), team formation, accountability, social skills, structures and structuring, distributed leadership, group autonomy, group processing, and face-to-face promotive interaction. Positive interdependence is "structuring group work so that in order for a group to succeed, all members in the group must meet their individual goals." Structures are "generic, content-free procedures that can be used for any subject at any age or proficiency level."
citation: Kluge, David. (1999). A Brief Introduction to Cooperative Learning. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED437840

article_title: Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Language Proficiency Acquisition, Assessment, and Communicative Behavior, Series B. Student Edition. Bilingual Education Teacher Training Packets.
title: Open-ended scenario: collaboratively planned, acted-out, and debriefed role play for language learners
description: The open-ended scenario is a pedagogical device designed by DiPietro (1981) that "resembles a role play in that it grows from a set of circumstances" but differs in that "the dialogues are planned collaboratively by the second-langage learn- ers, then acted out", after which interactions and transactions are discussed with the language facilitator. It unfolds in three phases: off-stage (planning and discussion), on-stage (acting out the dialogue), and a debriefing stage in which interactions and transactions are discussed. The packet provides guidelines for constructing open-ended scenarios, a guide to discussion on scenario development, and workshop activities in which trainees build and ev
citation: Calderon, Margarita; And Others. (1982). Methods and Techniques for Communicative Competence in Bilingual Education, Packet II. Language Proficiency Acquisition, Assessment, and Communicative Behavior, Series B. Student Edition. Bilingual Education Teacher Training Packets. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED226607

article_title: Teacher Metacognition within the Professional Learning Community
title: PLC facets that catalyze scholarship epistemology: trust, common goal, reflection opportunity, dialogue, and accountability for results
description: In contrast to traditional institutional epistemology where knowledge is transmitted from one person to another, the article describes scholarship epistemology as bringing together theory and practice and constructing new knowledge by working together. The facets of the PLC that catalyze this include "working in an environment of trust, having a common goal, creating an opportunity for reflection, becoming engaged in dialogue, and being accountable for results". This pattern names the structural conditions a PLC needs to foster deeper, metacognitive professional thinking.
citation: Prytula, M. P. (2012). Teacher Metacognition within the Professional Learning Community. International Education Studies. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n4p112

article_title: Characteristics of Professional Learning Communities in Mathematics: A Systematic Review
title: Mediating artifacts in mathematics PLC are selected according to the PLC's object
description: Across the reviewed studies, PLC used infrastructural frameworks (most commonly lesson studies and video clubs) plus operative-level artifacts such as video clips, classroom data, and mathematical problems. The review found "the artifacts used were selected depending on the object": artifacts for collaboration norms create safety, trust and participation; artifacts for understanding highlight mathematical concepts and strategies; artifacts for repertoire highlight aspects of mathematics teaching such as lesson plans, observations and student data. The same artifact type, e.g. video clips, can serve different objects depending on its content.
citation: Harvey, F., & Teledahl, A. (2022). Characteristics of Professional Learning Communities in Mathematics: A Systematic Review. Mathematics Teacher Education and Development, 24(1), 72–95. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1361397

article_title: Sea Turtle Trek, Hammocks Beach State Park: An Environmental Education Learning Experience Designed for Grades 6-8.
title: Pre-visit, on-site, post-visit field-trip activity arc
description: The Sea Turtle Trek packet structures a park field trip as three sequential activity phases: classroom preparation before the trip, hands-on activities conducted at the park, and classroom follow-up afterward. The guide states that "The packet includes three types of activities: 1) pre-visit activity 2) on-site activity 3) post-visit activity," with the on-site activities conducted at the park and the others in the classroom. The phases may be used together or separately.
citation: Bland, Samuel S. (1995). Sea Turtle Trek, Hammocks Beach State Park: An Environmental Education Learning Experience Designed for Grades 6-8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED401095

article_title: A New Framework for Teaching in the Cognitive Domain. ERIC Digest.
title: Problem-centered instruction with task-level engagement and problem progression
description: Within Merrill's framework, the problem-centered element holds that "Learning is promoted when learners are engaged in solving real-world problems." Its corollaries specify that learners are shown the tasks they will be able to do, are engaged at the problem or task level rather than just the operation or action level, and solve a progression of problems that are explicitly compared to one another. The digest presents these as the prescriptions for effective instruction supporting the framework's central problem element.
citation: Molenda, Michael. (2002). A New Framework for Teaching in the Cognitive Domain. ERIC Digest. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED470983

article_title: Exploring "DIALANG"'s Diagnostic Feedback in Online L2 Dynamic Assessment
title: Mediation typology of implicit-to-explicit moves in SCMC DA
description: Emerging from thematic analysis of the DA sessions, the mediation typology orders mediator moves from most implicit to most explicit. The article reports it "included four general categories, namely awareness raising, problem identification, overcoming the problem and finally, focusing on the structure". Moves include the virtual collaborative frame, auto smart edit, yellow and red highlighting, sharing relevant web links (cyber-mediation), choice offering, and oral explanation of target structures. Moves are employed individualized to learners' ZPD levels and reciprocity.
citation: Ebadi, S. (2016). Exploring DIALANG's Diagnostic Feedback in Online L2 Dynamic Assessment. Teaching English with Technology, 16(1), 41-58. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135925

article_title: Personal Inquiry: Orchestrating Science Investigations Within and Beyond the Classroom
title: Scripted Personally Meaningful Inquiry
description: This pattern operationalizes [Personal Inquiry](../theories/personal-inquiry.md)'s scripted-orchestration approach as a six-step activity sequence, implemented in the source study using the nQuire software toolkit. A persistent octagon diagram of the theory's 8-phase inquiry cycle is shown on every screen, functioning as both orientation ("where am I in this investigation?") and a navigable to-do list, and the software allows non-linear movement — students can return to revise a question or plan after collecting evidence. Teachers configure which phases and activities happen individually, in groups, at home, or in the field, and whether students see each other's data in real time or after th
citation: Sharples, M., Scanlon, E., Ainsworth, S., Anastopoulou, S., Collins, T., Crook, C., Jones, A., Kerawalla, L., Littleton, K., Mulholland, P., & O'Malley, C. (2015). Personal Inquiry: Orchestrating Science Investigations Within and Beyond the Classroom. *Journal of the Learning Sciences, 24*(2), 308-341. [https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2014.944642](https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2014.944642)

article_title: Educational Psychology, Unit 5: Facilitating Complex Thinking (Arduini-Van Hoose, 2020)
title: Socratic Seminar
description: Socratic Seminar is a structured, text-centered discussion pattern in which learners explore a complex question through dialogue, evidence, and follow-up questioning rather than through debate aimed at victory. The goal is disciplined interpretation: learners listen closely, build on one another's ideas, test assumptions, and return to the text or shared source as they refine understanding. The pattern works best when the prompt is open enough to sustain interpretation but bounded enough to keep the conversation tied to evidence. It is not just "having a discussion." The seminar requires preparation, facilitation, and norms that make inquiry through dialogue possible.
citation: Adler, M. J. (1982). *The Paideia proposal: An educational manifesto*. Macmillan.

article_title: Learning Practical Design Knowledge through Co-Designing Storyline Science Curriculum Units
title: Storyline Science Curriculum Design
description: Rather than sequencing a science unit around disciplinary topics, a storyline unit is organized around a coherent sequence of questions that students themselves raise in response to an anchoring phenomenon — the curriculum materials are written from the student's own perspective (using "we" pronouns: "we figure out," "we wonder about"), and each lesson's activities exist to answer a question the class has already asked, not to introduce content the curriculum has pre-decided is next. Standards coverage is achieved by backward design: only phenomena that require the target disciplinary ideas to explain are selected as anchors in the first place.

Cross-sectional, so it describes current patterns rather than accumulated change
Not designed for minors; readings must not drive consequential decisions

citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Citation-grounded behavioural item design with reverse scoring
description: PAUSE's items follow a reusable design pattern: every LLM-era item is anchored to a 2023-2026 paper, items are behavioural rather than dispositional, and roughly one third per domain are reverse-scored, since "Roughly one third of the items per domain (two or three of seven) are reverse-scored to counter acquiescence". All items include a not-applicable option, and unanswered items are dropped rather than imputed.

Probe non-responses must be scored as not applicable, never as uncritical acceptance
constraints: Anchors are supporting evidence for an item's framing, not validation of it
Several anchoring studies are recent preprints
Some items conflate early consultation with substitution, an imperfect proxy for whether reasoning stayed engaged

target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of AI-use behaviours across four offloading domains
examples: Item B5 renders the behavioural task, a Why this question panel, and a Reference panel quoting Dergaa et al. (2024) with a DOI

article_title: LLMs in text linguistics teaching: An exploratory study with genAI novices in higher education
citation: Nicola Brocca, Davide Garassino. (2026). LLMs in text linguistics teaching: an exploratory study with genAI novices in higher education. Computers and Education Open 11 (2026) 100414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100414
title: Pair-based, discovery-oriented LLM analysis activity following an eight-week disciplinary module
description: The intervention's design combined two pedagogical principles: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, realized through paired work, and Dewey's learning through experience, realized as an authentic discovery-oriented task without explicit prompt-engineering instruction. Students first completed an eight-week instructional module on text linguistics concepts, then manually analyzed a newspaper article, and finally used an LLM to verify their analysis, creating their own prompts and comparing AI-generated analysis with their own. The authors report that "students completed the assignment in pairs, allowing them to discuss prompting strategies, compare interpretations of LLM outputs, and jointly construct solutions". The activity was part of the course exam program and completed at home over two weeks.

access to LLMs via chatbot interfaces
constraints: Without expert scaffolding, students' prompting strategies remained limited, with little use of few-shot prompting or in-context examples

genAI novices
examples: Five pairs submitted reports analyzing an online newspaper article and comparing their analysis with ChatGPT-3.5, Gemini, or Perplexity outputs

article_title: Peer and AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR): A Human-Centered Approach to Formative Assessment
citation: Sperber, Lisa; MacArthur, Marit; Minnillo, Sophia; Stillman, Nicholas; Whithaus, Carl. (2025). Peer and AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR): A human-centered approach to formative assessment. Computers and Composition 76. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102921
title: PAIRR: peer review followed by rubric-driven AI feedback plus structured critical reflection
description: PAIRR is a formative-assessment sequence in which students draft, give and receive peer review, then prompt ChatGPT for feedback using an adapted prompt plus the instructor's rubric, and finally critically assess both kinds of feedback and reflect on revisions. Students are tasked with assessing AI feedback on their drafts, rather than taking it at face value, and determining if and how that feedback aligns with their writing goals. AI feedback comes after a complete draft to avoid interfering with drafting cognition and to discourage overreliance.

Scaffolded peer review prior to AI feedback
Guided practice and readings on ethical AI use and acknowledgment

AI may reflect linguistic and cultural biases present in LLM training data

target_learning_goals: Developing AI literacy and critical evaluation of AI outputs
Exercising writerly agency and metacognitive revision planning
examples: In the study, students in 10 writing and three large WI courses completed readings on AI and ethics, drafted, exchanged peer review, prompted ChatGPT with the rubric, assessed both feedback types, and revised with reflections on each source's role

article_title: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence
citation: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268
title: Pair coaching with group trainings and instructional materials rather than relying on coaching alone
description: The article's exploratory meta-analytic regressions indicate that coaching programs are more strongly associated with improved instruction and achievement when coaching is embedded in a broader PD package. Pairing coaching with group trainings was associated with larger effects on both outcomes, and pairing it with instructional resources such as curriculum was associated with "greater gains (0.21 SD larger)" on instruction. The authors interpret this as consistent with teachers building baseline skills before engaging directly with a coach.
requirements: Coaching must be combined with at least one complementary PD element such as group trainings, instructional content materials, or video libraries
constraints: These meta-analytic regressions are descriptive and do not capture the causal effect of a given program feature; limited statistical power prevents ruling out smaller relationships
target_learners: in-service pre-kindergarten through 12th grade teachers
examples: In the reviewed sample, 48 of 60 studies combined coaching with group trainings, 22 provided instructional content materials, and 14 supplemented coaching with video exemplars

article_title: Parental Involvement and Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Fan, X., Chen, M. (2001). Parental Involvement and Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009048817385
title: Parental involvement as a multidimensional construct whose components relate differently to achievement
description: The article treats parental involvement not as a unitary construct but as a set of distinguishable components — including parental aspiration/expectation for children's education achievement and parental home supervision — whose relationships with academic achievement differ in strength. Its moderator analysis organizes the quantitative literature around these components, finding that "parental aspiration/expectation for children's education achievement has the strongest relationship, whereas parental home supervision has the weakest relationship." It further distinguishes achievement measurement as global versus subject-specific, making indicator type a second organizing axis.
requirements: Empirical studies must operationalize parental involvement in distinguishable components and report quantitative relationships with achievement measures for the moderator synthesis to apply.
constraints: Component-level and indicator-type effect magnitudes are not printed in the available text; the framework is supported by the article's moderator analysis of the quantitative literature it synthesized.
target_learners: K-12 school students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement as measured by global indicators (e.g., GPA) and subject-specific indicators (e.g., math grades)
examples: The meta-analysis's moderator analysis ranked involvement components by relationship strength with achievement and compared global versus subject-specific achievement indicators.

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Participatory research as an umbrella research-to-action approach
description: The article defines participatory research (PR) as an "umbrella term for research designs, methods, and frameworks" that "use systematic inquiry in direct collaboration with those affected by the issue being studied for the purpose of action or change". PR replaces the "subjects" of traditional research with collaborators — stakeholders, community members, and end-users with insider knowledge and lived expertise — who share leadership in the research process. The article presents PR as valued across disciplines for solving complex problems and for producing research relevant to real-world contexts.
requirements: Direct engagement of local priorities and perspectives through partnerships between researchers and those with lived expertise of the issue
constraints: The specific PR approach and its nomenclature vary widely across disciplines
target_learners: Researchers new to participatory research
Community partners and stakeholders in collaborative inquiry
examples: The article describes an academic-community partnership using a citizen science approach to collect and interpret soil samples for environmental justice work

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: PARI methodology: a structured dyadic problem-solving interview for cognitive task analysis
description: The PARI (Precursor, Action, Result, Interpretation) methodology is a structured, thinking-aloud interview technique for cognitive task analysis of diagnostic problem solving, developed under the Basic Job Skills program. Per the report, "PARI: Precursor, (or reason for Action), Action, Result, and Interpretation (of result) are problem-solving components of interest in diagnostic tasks." Experts work in dyads: one poses a problem to a naive expert who generates a solution step by step while the first supplies results, followed by rehash sessions probing the reasons for decisions. The approach is grounded in studies of over 200 Air Force technicians in aircraft maintenance specialties whose primary task is troubleshooting.
requirements: A task analyst uses standardized interview questions and structured rehash sessions so data take a standard form comparable across specialties and skill levels
constraints: Developed for aircraft maintenance troubleshooting domains; the report states a future goal is examining generality to nonmaintenance problem-solving domains
target_learners: Air Force aircraft maintenance technicians learning troubleshooting
target_learning_goals: Adaptive troubleshooting and complex problem-solving skill in technical equipment maintenance
examples: Expert dyads solved representative samples of domain problems under realistic task performance conditions, with solutions elaborated in rehash sessions

article_title: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction.
citation: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-6499-1
title: PAL design framework: competency and interaction type as crucial design variables for pedagogical agents as learning companions
description: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions (PALs) are defined as "animated peer-like characters that simulate peer interaction in computer-based learning," grounded in social cognitive theory and peer modeling research. The framework identifies two crucial design variables: the PAL's competency (low vs. high domain knowledge, scripted as novice-like vs. advanced-peer comments) and interaction type (proactive initiation vs. responsive delivery only on request). The experiment showed these variables have different effects on learning, self-efficacy, and attitudes, so the framework treats PAL-learner relations as consistent with human peer relations.
requirements: The PAL must be perceived as peer-like and believable; equipping it with instructor-like advanced competency might undermine peer-likeness
constraints: The findings concern a single skill (instructional planning) over a limited time, and the PALs were prescripted rather than intelligent agents
target_learners: undergraduate novices in a task domain
target_learning_goals: recall and application of domain information; self-efficacy in the task; attitudes toward the agent
examples: The agent Mike, a casual-dressed peer in his early 20s, delivered either novice-like or advanced-peer scripts in a MIMIC-based instructional planning module within a 2x2 experiment

article_title: Effect of screen presentation on text reading and revising
citation: Annie Piolat, Jean-Yves Roussey and Olivier Thunin. (1997). Effects of screen presentation on text reading and revising. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies. https://doi.org/10.1006/ijhc.1997.0145
title: Page and Scroll screen-presentation prototypes
description: Two HyperTalk word-processing prototypes compared in both experiments. The Page prototype displayed the text page-by-page with numbered page icons, so "the position of the visible page relative to whole text was always available to participants". The Scroll prototype reproduced conventional scrolling with arrows but, in Experiment 1, deliberately omitted the scroll box, leaving users without an indication of their location in the text. Both showed the same window size and amount of text.

constraints: The display window was purposely made small (18 lines of about 50 characters) so a short 574-word document could be used with low processing load

target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and spatial encoding of text
revising and error correction in written texts

article_title: The Structure of Speed of Processing Across Cultures
citation: Papadopoulos, T. C., Georgiou, G. K., Deng, C., & Das, J. P. (2018). The Structure of Speed of Processing Across Cultures. Advances in Cognitive Psychology, 14(3), 112–125. https://doi.org/10.5709/acp-0243-7
title: PASS theory of intelligence: planning, attention, simultaneous, and successive processing as three cognitive systems
description: The PASS theory of intelligence proposes that cognition is organized in three systems: the planning system (executive functions for regulating and programming behavior, located in the frontal cortex), the attention-arousal system (focused, selective, sustained, effortful activity, located in the posterior parietal cortex), and a processing system including simultaneous coding (arranging information into a holistic pattern) and successive coding (coding information in discrete, serial order), located in posterior occipital, parietal, and temporal cortex. The study operationalized these processes with response-time measures adapted from the D-N CAS.
requirements: Operationalization requires tests consistent with the process of interest, such as the D-N CAS subtests used in this study
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: cognitive processing and assessment of intelligence
examples: The study used Matching Numbers and Planned Connections for planning, Expressive Attention and Number Detection for attention, Matrices and Verbal-Spatial Relations for simultaneous, and Word Series and Sentence Questions for successive processing.

article_title: Is approximate number precision a stable predictor of math ability?
citation: Libertus Melissa E., Feigenson Lisa, Halberda Justin. (2013). Is Approximate Number Precision a Stable Predictor of Math Ability? Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2013.02.001
title: Panamath non-symbolic numerical comparison task for assessing ANS acuity in young children
description: Panamath (the Psychophysical Assessment of Numerical Approximation) is a non-symbolic numerical comparison task administered as a free-download software tool. Children see spatially separated blue and yellow dot arrays on a laptop screen and indicate which color has more dots; arrays are visible for 2000 ms, with accuracy and response time recorded via an experimenter keypress. In this study children completed six practice trials followed by 60 test trials with dot numbers from 4 to 15 across four ratio bins, controlling for dot size and cumulative surface area across trial halves.
requirements: An experimenter blind to the screen who records verbal responses to capture response time
Familiarization trials with auditory feedback so children understand the task
constraints: Split-half reliability in this preschool sample was 0.65 at Time 1 and 0.72 at Time 2; the psychophysical model did not yield a reliable w fit for some participants
target_learners: preschool-aged children
examples: Used at both time points of the longitudinal study; dots ranged from 4 to 15 with ratio bins 1:2, 2:3, 3:4, and 6:7

Audiences (administrators, councils) are available to receive student findings

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing individual mental representations: group members possess sufficiently similar mental representations they externalize and compare
description: This commonsensical paradigm holds that shared knowledge in a small group means each member possesses the same knowledge, elaborated as "mental representations that are sufficiently similar to specific mental representations of each of the other members." Sharing is a matter of transferring and comparing ideas in ways that typically do not change the ideas. The editorial links it to Clark and Brennan's classic grounding analysis, in which collaborators externalize propositional expressions of their representations.
requirements: Individuals possess well-formed opinions and can unproblematically express them
constraints: Assumes sharing typically does not change the ideas being shared
target_learners: Small collaborating groups
target_learning_goals: Establishing common ground through externalizing and comparing ideas
examples: The editorial cites the grounding analysis of Clark and Brennan (1991), often cited in CSCL research, as this paradigm's classic elaboration

citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing an object: shared knowledge arises from a group's joint orientation toward a common object of work
description: This paradigm conceives shared knowledge as "a natural consequence of a group being collaboratively involved with the object of their work together": all members are oriented toward the same artifact, problem, or goal and thereby come to share knowledge of it. Once the object is truly shared, no special coordination is needed. The editorial cites analyses of students defining and sharing multiple realizations of a mathematical object and of affordances of an object being enacted interactively.
requirements: The object must be truly shared among participants
target_learners: Student groups collaborating online or in classrooms
target_learning_goals: Constructing new shared knowledge about a common object of work
examples: A cited ijCSCL article (Çakır et al. 2009) describes an online group whose construction of new shared knowledge, such as formulating an algebraic expression, proceeded quickly once all members could see the same mathematical object

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing a situation: engagement in collaborative discourse within a common context automatically generates shared knowledge

The editorial states that according to this paradigm, "the engagement in collaborative discourse can automatically generate shared knowledge as an ongoing process," with situation and discourse standing in a mutually constitutive relationship.

target_learning_goals: Generating shared knowledge through collaborative discourse
examples: The editorial cites Duranti and Goodwin's claim that talk and context shape each other, and Roschelle and Teasley's joint problem space construct

citation: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7

article_title: Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction
citation: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3
title: Participatory design as a three-phase user-involvement approach to instructional re/design
description: Participatory design, imported from fields such as cognitive ergonomics and health promotion, aims to ensure active participation of users in design decisions that affect them. The article states that a participatory design process consists of three phases: "analysis", "design", and "implementation" — participants first analyze the current situation and its shortcomings, then generate ideas for re/design, and finally devise an implementation plan. In this study the approach was adapted for secondary students co-designing their courses with their teacher.

constraints: The article notes participatory design in school contexts is fairly new and that it found hardly any prior classroom studies of its effects

target_learning_goals: Improving the fit of instruction to students' perceptions and desires

description: The article's methodological contribution is a taxonomy of structural equation models for directional ordering, extending Muthén and Asparouhov's contemporaneous-effects models with latent measurement factors, lag2 paths, random intercepts, and covariate strategies. title: PASH: the personality–achievement saturation hypothesis framework
description: PASH (personality–achievement saturation hypothesis; Hübner et al., 2022) is a framework describing when personality manifests more strongly in achievement measures.
