article_title: Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial
citation: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7
title: Design early practice schedules so that successive skills share abstract parsing-rule structure, since this structure generalizes within seconds
description: The article concludes that "our results document parsing structure generalization in the very early stages of skill learning (i.e., within-seconds and after a single trial of practice)" and states "This information may be useful for improving the design of practice schedules in the context of sports, music, and physical rehabilitation." Sequencing a second skill to share abstract event cues (e.g., starting and ending with the same element) with a just-practiced first skill leverages one-trial generalization, whereas sharing only ordinal or transition structure does not.
requirements: The two skills must share a parsing rule structure (e.g., sequences starting and ending with the same keypress) for early generalization to occur
constraints: Generalization was demonstrated for 5-item keypress sequences over seconds-long timescales; the article notes the impact of sequence difficulty and sequence length on generalization remains to be addressed, and the double-tap compression effect "may be attenuated as the sequence length increases"
target_learners: adults practicing sequential motor skills in sports, music, or physical rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: accelerated learning of related new skills through generalization from prior practice
examples: Participants who practiced sequence 4-1-3-2-4 for one 10-second trial showed higher onset performance on skill B sequences sharing the start-end parsing rule than on those sharing only transitions
key_sources: B. P. Johnson, I. Iturrate, R. Y. Fakhreddine, M. Bönstrup, E. R. Buch, E. M. Robertson and L. G. Cohen. (2023). Generalization of procedural motor sequence learning after a single practice trial. npj Science of Learning 8:45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00194-7

article_title: Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning
citation: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5
title: Time-resolved Paired Associative Learning paradigm with rhythmic tone-flash sensory entrainment
description: A novel PAL paradigm in which each trial begins with 16 transient task-irrelevant tone-flash stimuli presented "brieﬂy (30 ms) and isochronously at a rate of 5 Hz ... or 10 Hz" before a novel speech-print pair, followed by dense sampling of stimulus onset asynchronies (200–980 ms, 20 ms steps) so that frequency-dependent behavioral effects of rhythmic stimulation can be measured. Five pseudo-phones crossed with five Korean characters generated the learning stimuli, learned via feedback over 10 blocks of 80 trials. A null-stimulation control task replaced entrainment with a single salient visual stimulus.
requirements: A unimodal familiarization phase ensuring successful recognition (> 70%) of the learning materials before associative learning.
constraints: Studied with right-handed native Chinese speakers with no Korean experience; the design does not include EEG, which the authors say is needed for fine-grained temporal dynamics.
target_learners: healthy adults learning novel speech-print mappings
target_learning_goals: paired associative learning of speech sounds and written symbols
examples: Thirty-six participants were randomly assigned to one stimulation condition; a separate group of 25 completed the Null-stimulation control task.
key_sources: Zhijun Liao, Xiya Ao, Yulu Sun, Manli Zhang & Xiangzhi Meng. (2024). Alpha sensory stimulation modulates theta phase during speech-print associative learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00263-5

article_title: A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms
citation: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305
title: Paired model-tracing and constraint-based tutors for statistical hypothesis testing
description: The article's empirical artifact is a pair of intelligent tutoring systems built by the authors: "a model-tracing and constraint-based tutor for the same problem domain (statistical hypothesis testing)". Building both tutors for one domain allowed the authors to evaluate proponents' claims, contrast the two approaches, and derive guidance for other intelligent tutoring system builders.
requirements: Both tutors were built for the same problem domain to enable direct comparison
constraints: Findings are drawn from one problem domain, statistical hypothesis testing
target_learners: students learning statistical hypothesis testing
examples: The authors report on their findings from the paired tutors with the goals of evaluating proponents' claims and providing guidance for others building intelligent tutoring systems.
key_sources: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305

article_title: Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings
citation: Olga C. Santos, Milos Kravcik, Jesus G. Boticario. (2016). Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:809–820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0114-z
title: PALE workshop series (2011–2015) as a body of personalization research
description: The Personalization Approaches in Learning Environments (PALE) workshop series has been "run each year at the UMAP conference ever since 2011". The article analyses "A total of 39 contributions" from the first five editions (2011 to 2015) in terms of the three research aspects, covering intelligent tutoring systems, educational recommender systems, learning management systems, personal learning environments, educational games, agent-based environments, multi-user virtual environments and ad-hoc approaches. It served as the catalyst for this special issue.
requirements: Annual co-location with the UMAP conference to sustain the research community
target_learners: researchers and practitioners in user modelling and AIED
target_learning_goals: advancing user modelling to support personalization in learning environments
examples: Interaction sources covered include observations, mice, videocameras, touch gestures, social interactions, eye-tracking and physiological sensors; devices include mobiles, tablets and tabletops.
key_sources: Olga C. Santos, Milos Kravcik, Jesus G. Boticario. (2016). Preface to Special Issue on User Modelling to Support Personalization in Enhanced Educational Settings. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:809–820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0114-z

article_title: Measuring learning in serious games: a case study with structural assessment
citation: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0
title: Pathfinder network technique for structural assessment
description: Pathfinder is a graph-theoretic distance technique that represents a proximity matrix in a graphical network structure (PFnet). It uses the distance measured by the minimum number of links connecting two nodes in a graph. The algorithm removes direct links if a shorter, indirect path connects both concepts. Pathfinder was adopted because it does not force a hierarchical structure on the data and identifies meaningful links between concepts.
requirements: A proximity matrix of relatedness ratings between concept pairs
A scaling procedure to transform ratings into a network representation
constraints: When participants use many extreme relatedness ratings, Pathfinder includes all links when there are tied distances, producing networks with many more links than expected
target_learners: Learners in complex-skill domains
key_sources: Wouters, P., van der Spek, E. D., & van Oostendorp, H. (2011). Measuring learning in serious games: A case study with structural assessment. Educational Technology Research and Development, 59(6), 741–763. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9183-0

article_title: Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3
title: Make phase-related part-tasks explicit and sequenced and provide part-task-congruent external representations for each phase
description: The article's design implication is that complex learning-task completion is facilitated when the different phase-related part-tasks are made explicit and properly sequenced, and part-task congruent ERs are provided. Using multiple ERs can provide different perspectives of the knowledge domain and, when properly matched to the task demands and activities, their complementary function can gradually increase student understanding and phase-related part-task activity. The study's match condition implemented this by delivering a conceptual, causal and simulation ER in phased order.
requirements: Part-task congruent ERs (i.e., domain specific content schemes) must be provided for each phase-related part-task
The part-tasks must be made explicit and properly sequenced
constraints: The effect of the design of representational scripting does not automatically apply to all complex learning-tasks; it depends on the characteristics of the problem and the involved knowledge domains
target_learners: non-expert students collaboratively carrying out complex learning-tasks in CSCL environments
examples: Groups in the match condition received the conceptual ER for problem orientation, the causal ER for problem solution and the simulation ER for solution evaluation, and outperformed the conceptual and simulation mismatch conditions on total task performance
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2010). Design and effects of representational scripting on group performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-010-9148-3

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: Involve teachers as partners in participatory design when building teacher-facing learning analytics tools
description: The study argues that participatory design, which actively engages users as partners influencing design choices and trade-offs, produces educational tools grounded in teachers' needs, abilities, and classroom contexts. The article states that "participatory design enhances both the technical soundness and pedagogical strength of educational tools, supporting successful adoption". The study operationalized this through iterative focus groups and a KANO questionnaire feeding directly into prototype design decisions.
requirements: Iterative cycles of investigating, reflecting, and learning collaboratively with teachers through activities such as focus groups and structured evaluation
constraints: Rigor in participatory design is defined by teachers' goals and expressed as internal validity of a well-structured process account rather than experimental standards
target_learners: primary school students
examples: Two design rounds: five focus groups (19 participants) generating indicators and features, then a KANO questionnaire (45 teachers) refining priorities that guided the prototype
key_sources: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z

article_title: Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions
citation: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x
title: Participation style in online instructional discussions as a two-dimensional construct of participation reasons (Why) and participation forms (How)
description: The article defines participation style as the sum of individualistic characteristics explaining participation in online discussions, structured in two dimensions. The Why dimension comprises the main motivators of participation, while the How dimension comprises items expressing participation behaviors or forms. The authors state: "The Why dimension comprises the main motivators of the participants' participation in online instructional environments, whereas the How dimension comprises items expressing participation behaviors or forms." This mirrors Kolb's learning-style inventory logic of pairing a preference for receiving information with a preference for transforming it, applied here to online discussion participation.
requirements: The scale is intended for individuals who have actually participated in online instructional discussions; participants who stated they had never participated were excluded from both study groups
constraints: The study groups consisted of undergraduate and graduate students at Turkish universities, mainly in Computer Education and Instructional Technologies departments
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students participating in online instructional discussions
target_learning_goals: identifying learners' participation styles in online discussion environments to support more effective learning
examples: The scale was applied to undergraduate and graduate students at 15 and 24 Turkish universities across two datasets
key_sources: Pala Ferhat Kadir, Erdem Mukaddes. (2020). Development of a participation style scale for online instructional discussions. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09817-x

article_title: The parents' tale: Why parents resist the educational use of smartphones at schools?
citation: Hadad, S., Meishar-Tal, H., & Blau, I. (2020). The parents' tale: Why parents resist the educational use of smartphones at schools?. Computers & Education, 157, 103984. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103984
title: Integrated framework of parental resistance to educational technology combining resistance levels, four resistance factors, parenting styles and demographics
description: The article proposes an integrated framework (Figure 1) linking levels of actual parental resistance (no, passive, active) to four resistance factors — social, environmental, economic and pedagogical — plus parenting styles and demographic variables. It builds on the "Three Pillars of Technological Rejection" model, whose "model contains three types of reasons for rejecting technologies: social, economic and environmental", adding the pedagogical factor. "The study introduced and empirically tested an integrated framework for the examination of parental resistance to the educational use of smartphones".
requirements: Measures of resistance level, the four resistance factors, and parenting styles, as operationalised in the study's questionnaires
constraints: Developed and tested in the context of parental resistance to smartphones in Israeli schools
target_learners: School students whose parents respond to school technology policies
target_learning_goals: Integration of mobile technologies into school learning
examples: Applied in a survey of 220 Israeli parents, with the framework tested via ANOVA, chi-square and regression analyses
key_sources: Hadad, S., Meishar-Tal, H., & Blau, I. (2020). The parents' tale: Why parents resist the educational use of smartphones at schools?. Computers & Education, 157, 103984. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103984

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Parasocial interaction is an asymmetrical, multidimensional process during media reception
description: The thesis describes the theory of parasocial interaction (PSI; Horton & Wohl, 1956; Hartmann, Schramm, & Klimmt, 2004b) as a framework for how social entities influence learners during video reception. PSI is "described as the conversational give and take between a persona (i.e. the social entity) and a recipient," and "the interaction is asymmetrical, since the persona acts independently from the cognitions, emotions, and behavior of the learner." The Two-Level Model holds PSI strength depends on characteristics of the personae and recipients, with perceptive-cognitive, affective, and behavioral facets.
requirements: A persona presented medially with no return channel; recipient characteristics and persona characteristics determine PSI strength
constraints: Only processes during media consumption are relevant; parasocial relationships are treated as separate constructs and not described further
target_learners: learners receiving instruction via video
target_learning_goals: attention, evaluation processes, and engagement with learning material
key_sources: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001

article_title: Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes
citation: Hughes, A., Gerson, S. A., & van Schaik, J. E. (2026). Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes. Computers & Education, 242: 105510. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105510
title: Pair classroom robot curricula with concise hands-on teacher education for significant impact
description: The article recommends embedding programming with robots in primary education alongside targeted teacher education, underscoring "the importance of teacher education for significant impact". A 3-h workshop covering programming concepts, hands-on robot practice, and curriculum integration discussion, delivered before classroom implementation, was associated with significant pupil and teacher gains that the robot curriculum alone did not produce. The authors state these findings "offer practical guidance for embedding programming with robots in primary education".
requirements: Teachers attend a hands-on education workshop covering programming concepts, robot practice, and curriculum integration before implementing the robot curriculum
constraints: The workshop effect was demonstrated with a 3-h session paired with a 6-week Cubetto curriculum in Welsh early primary classrooms; the article notes unequal teacher sample sizes across conditions may limit generalisability
target_learners: Early primary school teachers (of pupils aged 4–7)
target_learning_goals: Teaching programming and computational thinking with educational robots
examples: Teachers in Intervention+ attended a 3-h robot workshop led by two researchers including a presentation on programming concepts, hands-on Cubetto practice, and discussions on incorporating programming into existing curricula
key_sources: Hughes, A., Gerson, S. A., & van Schaik, J. E. (2026). Teacher-led robot intervention in early primary school classrooms improves pupil and teacher outcomes. Computers & Education, 242: 105510. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105510

article_title: IDR: A participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning
citation: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043
title: Participatory pattern design by distributed interdisciplinary teams
description: The article describes a reusable design arrangement in which a distributed, interdisciplinary team collaboratively produces design patterns. The team 'developed a set of over 120 design patterns' using an open source web toolkit, reflecting, in the authors' words, 'the participatory nature of pattern design'. This pattern makes the design patterns tradition the shared medium through which researchers, developers and teachers contribute.
requirements: A distributed team spanning educational research, software development and teaching expertise; a shared toolkit for authoring patterns
target_learners: educational researchers
software developers
teachers
examples: a pan-European project team of educational researchers, software developers and teachers developed over 120 design patterns
key_sources: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043

article_title: A network analysis on digital media use, reading enjoyment, and orthography precision in a highly educated sample
citation: Miccoli, L., Arias, M. Á. P., & Santiago, J. (2023). A network analysis on digital media use, reading enjoyment, and orthography precision in a highly educated sample. Computers & Education, 207, 104932. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104932
title: Partial correlation network analysis as a data-driven method for examining multifactorial relations between variables
description: The article relies on regularized partial correlation network analysis (graphical LASSO, EBICglasso), "a recently emerging tool that can reveal both the direct and indirect relations between variables". It is data-driven, does not require hypothesizing latent factors, and provides a graphical display of relations and association strengths. Centrality measures (strength, closeness, betweenness) describe node importance, and bootstrapping assesses network accuracy and stability via CS-coefficients.
requirements: Sample size estimations (power analysis) are pivotal to maximize sensitivity and reduce false negatives given LASSO regularization favors specificity over sensitivity
constraints: The article states there is no consensus on a unique way to assess network goodness of fit
target_learners: adults in post-secondary education
key_sources: Miccoli, L., Arias, M. Á. P., & Santiago, J. (2023). A network analysis on digital media use, reading enjoyment, and orthography precision in a highly educated sample. Computers & Education, 207, 104932. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104932

article_title: Effects of school-based physical activity on mathematics performance in children: a systematic review.
citation: Sneck S., Viholainen H., Syväoja H., Kankaapää A., Hakonen H., Poikkeus A.-M., Tammelin T. (2019). Effects of school-based physical activity on mathematics performance in children: a systematic review. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-019-0866-6
title: Mechanisms account proposing that PA affects mathematics performance via brain and cognition, executive functions, motor-cognitive development, and emotional engagement
description: The review organises candidate mediating mechanisms for PA effects on mathematics into several strands: brain structure and function effects, executive functions (inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility) that are associated with mathematics achievement, motor development and related cognitive skills such as visuospatial skills and rapid automatized naming, and emotional experiences linked to mathematical achievement including math anxiety. The review notes "the findings on links between PA interventions and cognitive performance in children are still relatively rare and inconsistent" and calls for merging neuroscientific, psychological and educational theorizing.
requirements: Further examination of cognitive skills, executive functions, behaviour and brain activation outcomes in future intervention studies to determine how or why PA might affect mathematics performance
constraints: The mechanisms remain hypothesised; the review reports that findings on links between PA interventions and cognitive performance are rare and inconsistent
target_learners: Children aged 4–16
target_learning_goals: Mathematics performance and underlying cognitive and emotional mediators
examples: The review cites a study in which children's motor skills explained almost 16% of the variation in mathematical measures, and one reporting increased prefrontal cortex activity after exercise
key_sources: Sneck S., Viholainen H., Syväoja H., Kankaapää A., Hakonen H., Poikkeus A.-M., Tammelin T. (2019). Effects of school-based physical activity on mathematics performance in children: a systematic review. The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-019-0866-6

article_title: Physically Active Lessons: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Miller, S., Gildea, A., Sloan, S., & Thurston, A. (2015). Physically Active Lessons: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Physically Active Lessons (PAL) programme
description: PAL is a classroom-based primary-school intervention, adapted from the US PAAC programme (which evolved from Take 10!) by a University of Bristol team for the UK context. As the report describes it, "PAL is a classroom -based intervention that is delivered by teachers to primary school pupils. It integrates short bouts of physical activity with academic content related to literacy and numeracy." It aims to add a minimum of 90 minutes of physical activity per week in sessions of roughly 10–15 minutes twice daily, Monday to Friday, while boosting attainment through improved cognitive function. In the pilot it cost an estimated £9.08 per pupil in the first year, or £3.02 per pupil per year over three years, with no ongoing school costs after training.
requirements: Teachers develop and adapt activities through a collaborative enquiry framework supported by the Teacher Development Trust, sharing resources via an online portal and forum
constraints: At the time of the evaluation the programme was not manualised and was still in development, so it was not ready for an efficacy or effectiveness trial
target_learners: Year 4 and Year 5 primary school pupils
examples: In the pilot, teachers were trained in January 2014 by a specialist physical education consultant and delivered the programme from February to July 2014; example activities included star jumps while recalling times tables during numeracy lessons
key_sources: Miller, S., Gildea, A., Sloan, S., & Thurston, A. (2015). Physically Active Lessons: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581164

article_title: 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Lord, P., Rabiasz, A., and Styles, B. (2017). 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN84508118
title: Passive 'push' dissemination of evidence-based materials alone is insufficient to change pupil outcomes; schools need support to navigate, prioritise and apply research information
description: The evaluators conclude that simply sending research summaries and evidence-based resources to schools is not an effective way to improve pupil outcomes, even when materials are well structured and include examples for practice. They suggest "if schools had support to navigate and prioritise that information, greater impact could be achieved" and that schools may need help transforming materials into classroom change. This principle is grounded in a null result from a very high-security trial, so it is a boundary on dissemination, not a tested recipe for support.
requirements: Any dissemination effort aiming at practice change should be accompanied by support beyond passive sending of materials, per the authors' interpretation of the null result
constraints: The trial did not monitor engagement or control-group business as usual; the recommended supported approaches were not tested in this trial but in the accompanying Evidence-based Literacy Support trial
target_learners: Primary school teachers and headteachers in England
target_learning_goals: Evidence-informed literacy teaching practice; Key Stage 2 literacy attainment
examples: All four providers' materials included applicability elements (top tips, practice recommendations, interactive visual guides, school-presenter videos), yet none moved attainment
key_sources: Lord, P., Rabiasz, A., and Styles, B. (2017). 'Literacy Octopus' Dissemination Trial: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN84508118

article_title: Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context
citation: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1566
title: Pair metacognitive strategy instruction with books of literary quality appropriate to children's developmental levels
description: The article's central design recommendation is that reading comprehension instruction combine metacognitive strategy with children's literature of literary quality: "students should use metacognitive strategy along with books of literary quality to improve reading comprehension skills". Books must suit children's developmental levels and be prepared with artistic sensitivity, while strategy instruction spans pre-, during-, and post-reading. The quasi-experiment's post-test and ANCOVA results are offered as support.
requirements: Books must be appropriate for children's developmental levels and of literary quality; strategy instruction must include planning, self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and self-regulation phases
constraints: Durability of metacognitive skill gains is unknown; the study covered only 5th grade and five books from the 100 Basic Works
target_learners: primary/early secondary students (grades 5, ages 10-12) in language arts
examples: Over 8 weeks, experimental students read five award-winning literary-quality books with the three-phase metacognitive instruction, while controls read five 100 Basic Works books conventionally
key_sources: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Improving Reading Comprehension Skills with Children's Books through Metacognitive Strategy: The Turkish Context. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i9.1566

article_title: Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too!
citation: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164
title: Paivio's dual coding theory
description: The article presents dual coding theory as the principal theoretical rationale for using pictures in reading instruction. According to the theory, "the human cognition consists of two systems that process knowledge simultaneously, one processing the nonverbal objects (Imagery) and one dealing with language (verbal)", with words and images having different cognitive representations. Building on it, Mayer proposes learners can construct representational and referential connections between verbal and visual materials. The study invokes this framework to predict that adding pictures gives readers a second information source.
requirements: Presentation of verbal and visual materials together so that connections between representations can be constructed
constraints: Introduced in the article as background theory, not tested directly
target_learners: University EFL students in ESP reading courses
examples: The experimental passages were furnished with different kinds of pictures so learners could draw on both verbal and imagery systems while reading.
key_sources: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164

article_title: The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate
citation: Mohsen Alikhani & Esmaeil Bagheridoust. (2017). The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p44
title: Use pair work and group work in EFL speaking classes to raise willingness to communicate
description: The article recommends that instructors involve language learners in pair work and group work, since in Iranian language schools most speaking tasks were done individually or with little group work, which adversely affected class atmosphere and WTC. It argues that "teachers use such activities because they increase the amount of language input (McGroarty, 1993) as well as output (Long & Porter, 1985)", and that the study's findings show GDOI strategies improved WTC and speaking ability.
requirements: Instructors must be aware of GDOI; the article attributes underuse of group work to instructors not being aware of it
constraints: The article acknowledges GDOI would suffer some limitations, which learners contended might hinder the benefits they could avail from such L2 teaching strategies
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in language institutes
examples: The experimental group received GDOI with maximum pair and group interaction over one semester and outperformed the conventionally taught control group on both posttests
key_sources: Mohsen Alikhani & Esmaeil Bagheridoust. (2017). The Effect of Group Dynamics-Oriented Instruction on Developing Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Ability and Willingness to Communicate. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p44

article_title: Examining the Role of Pre-Instruction Academic Performance within a Text-Based Approach to Improving Student Content Knowledge and Understanding
citation: Jeanne Wanzek, Greg Roberts, Sharon Vaughn, Elizabeth Swanson, and Katherine Sargent. (2019). Examining the Role of Pre-Instruction Academic Performance Within A Text-based Approach to Improving Student Content Knowledge and Understanding. Exceptional Children, 85(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918783187
title: PACT (Promoting Adolescents' Comprehension of Text) instructional practices for middle school social studies
description: PACT is a set of text-based instructional practices integrated within social studies content units. It is "intended to be integrated within social studies content units to increase engagement of all students in supported text-based learning, discourse-based processes, and application of newly learned content." In this study teachers delivered three 10-day U.S. history units using semi-scripted lesson plans, with coaches supporting implementation at least weekly. The program was evaluated in a class-level randomized trial against typical instruction using the same content.
requirements: Teachers received a one-day eight-hour professional development workshop on implementing each PACT component before instruction, plus assigned coach support during the three units.
constraints: The article notes the robustness of results may be possible only when at least the observed fidelity levels and amount of instructional support are received.

description: PA-driven instruction is teaching that ensures learners apply relevant previous knowledge and abilities to solve open-ended mathematics problems with the teacher as a facilitator, so that students demonstrate proficiency in solving mathematical problems. constraints: In this study the performance assessment tasks were not extended projects; each test lasted two hours
target_learners: senior high school Form 1 science students in Ghana
examples: Two intact Form 1 classes at Ghana National College were assigned by coin toss to PA-driven instruction or traditional instruction for six weeks, with 320 minutes of mathematics per week

Components designed to be used together, not in isolation

citation: Shaffer, S. C., Eshbach, B. E., & Santiago-Blay, J. A. (2015). A Dual Approach to Fostering Under-Prepared Student Success: Focusing on Doing and Becoming. InSight: A Journal of Scholarly Teaching, 10. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gK5I_68g0X8

description: A six-credit paired course design in which under-prepared first-year students are simultaneously enrolled in a reading support course and a content course, so that reading skills and study strategies taught in the reading course are applied directly to the content course material. The article frames this as a dual approach addressing both "academic skills, labeled as 'doing', and lifelong learning, called 'becoming'". Instructional time in the reading course was divided equally between the two strands, and the content course remained a traditional lecture-based course.

Faculty coordination to structure assignments applying reading-course strategies to the paired content course

examples: Fifteen first-year students took a three-credit reading course meeting twice weekly alongside a three-credit environmental science course meeting once weekly; 18 students taking only environmental science served as controls for ELLI comparisons

title: Hoover-Dempsey model of parent involvement motivation extended with perceived staff care and trust
description: The article applies the Hoover-Dempsey and Sandler account in which involvement is motivated by "how parents construct their role for parent involvement" and by parents' beliefs in their own effectiveness, supplemented by invitations from school, teachers, and child, and by perceived life context. citation: Gambari, I. A. & Yusuf, M. O. (2016). Effects of Computer-Assisted Jigsaw II Cooperative Learning Strategy on Physics Achievement and Retention. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(4), 352-367. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1116981
title: Jigsaw II home group and expert group rotation with computer-assisted content
description: This instructional pattern structures cooperative learning around a two-stage group rotation supported by computer-assisted instruction. Students are divided into small heterogeneous "home groups, with three members in each group", where each member is assigned a different portion of the lesson content. After initial study of basic concepts, members move to expert groups consisting of peers assigned the same portion, where they "discussed and shared their particular materials with other members of the group and discussed how to teach it to their members in the home group". Teammates then return to home groups to teach what they learned, with a second expert group meeting held to clarify doubts and misconceptions before re-teaching.
requirements: Heterogeneous grouping with three members per home group
Lesson content divided into portions matching the number of home group members
Time allocated for both expert group and home group meetings
constraints: Group processing forms must be completed after each lesson to monitor group behaviour
target_learners: Senior secondary school students in heterogeneous classes
target_learning_goals: Understanding and retention of physics concepts through peer teaching
examples: In the study, students studied assigned tasks using the Computer-Assisted Learning Package, with each member attempting to learn the assigned task as an expert by referring to the computer package and available resources.

citation: Pagan, S., & Sénéchal, M. (2014). Involving Parents in a Summer Book Reading Program to Promote Reading Comprehension, Fluency, and Vocabulary in Grade 3 and Grade 5 Children. Canadian Journal of Education, 37(2). http://www.cje-rce.ca

constraints: Effects not yet replicated in larger-scale studies; the comprehensive design does not allow attribution to specific components

examples: Structure-oriented teaching of the particle concept assisted by the courseware preceded teaching of changing states of matter in the study

description: The article argues that pathology training, despite defaulting to passive learning, is ideally suited for active approaches because the daily practice of pathology — reaching a final diagnosis with pattern recognition as the main tool — "can very easily be simulated by quizzes and tests, making gamification an extremely appealing strategy for teachers in this field". title: PA-PBL: peer-tutor-facilitated problem-based learning with clinical history-taking simulation
description: PA-PBL is a blended model in which problem-based learning sessions are facilitated by trained same-grade peer tutors and added to standard lectures. Groups of "8-12 students were formed, with a peer tutor in the same grade who had underwent preparatory training prior to the activity's initiation." Each round runs four phases: preparation with department-approved cases, about 90 minutes of problem exploration in which students simulate clinical consultations and ask the peer tutor questions as they would a patient, one week of self-directed learning, and about 60 minutes of knowledge sharing with whiteboard presentations reviewed by researchers. In the trial it supplemented lectures in the Infection and Immunity module across four rounds in one academic year.

Recorded discussions reviewed by researchers to ensure quality
constraints: Implementing PA-PBL incurs higher costs than lecture-based learning due to peer tutor training and small-group coordination resources
target_learners: second-year undergraduate clinical medicine students
examples: Four rounds of PA-PBL, twice each semester, delivered to 134 volunteers alongside standard lectures in the Infection and Immunity module

citation: Modrau B, Kirk KF, Said SMA, Bjarkam CR, Sunde L, Bodilsen J, Dal J, Kristensen JK, Emmersen J, Astorp MB, Andersen S. (2025). Pass/Fail Versus Tiered Grades and Academic Performance in Undergraduate Medical Education: Crossover Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/74975
title: Choose Pass/Fail grading in high-stakes exams when well-being is prioritized, accepting a shift in examiner focus toward upholding standards
description: The authors conclude that a shift from Tiered grades to Pass/Fail "causes a shift in focus from rewarding high performance to upholding standards among underperforming medical students." Because Pass/Fail evaluations correlate with enhanced well-being and reduced stress, they argue "Pass/Fail may be preferred over Tiered grade assessments in high-stakes exams." The principle accepts a higher recorded fail rate as the cost of a less competitive learning environment.
requirements: Requires examiners and study boards to understand that Pass/Fail grading redirects attention to ensuring underperforming students meet standards rather than rewarding high achievers
constraints: The higher fail rate under Pass/Fail leveled out when the near-fail Tiered grade was counted as Fail; final licensing exam performance was unchanged; findings come from a single center with high-achieving medical students
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical years
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic standards at clinical competency exams while supporting student well-being
examples: Aalborg University's 2018 curriculum reform switched fifth-year exams from Tiered grades to Pass/Fail while keeping learning objectives, module organization, and teaching principles unaltered, providing the natural experiment analyzed in this study

description: The article's conceptual framework defines palliative care communication skill as an individual's evaluative, relatively stable psychological attitude expressed in specific behaviors toward particular entities. title: Pair immersive virtual guidance with authentic tactile practice on physical phantoms to preserve haptic fidelity in surgical simulation training
description: The article argues that purely virtual systems cannot replicate real surgical tactility, while AR overlays alone lack immersive hands-on practice; IMR-SS resolves this by letting trainees "use actual instruments on a tangible model while receiving holographic feedback." The authors state this high-fidelity tactile interaction may enhance training realism and improve skill transfer to the operating room, consistent with evidence that adding haptic feedback in simulation improves technical performance outcomes. The trial's IMR group practiced on a patient-specific phantom with real instruments while receiving aligned holographic guidance.
requirements: Patient-specific physical phantoms, real surgical instruments, and spatial tracking that keeps tactile practice synchronized with virtual cues
constraints: Purely software-based VR trainers have lower marginal cost but sacrifice haptic realism; the approach balances fidelity with affordability at approximately US$4,500 hardware and roughly US$0.50 materials per case
target_learners: novice surgical trainees lacking hands-on opportunities
target_learning_goals: psychomotor surgical skills with authentic haptic feedback
examples: The hands-on module used a modular lumbar phantom reconstructed from patient CT data with replaceable PLA vertebrae reproducing human bone mechanics, tracked by a binocular camera

title: Two-axis classification of paid e-learning resources by intent of use and mode of presentation
description: The article proposes classifying paid e-learning resources along two axes to understand students' justifications for use. By intent, resources are "Preparatory resources, intended solely for board exam preparation" versus general extracurricular content that assists in assimilating medical education without being tied to a specific curriculum or exam. By presentation, resources are visual (video- and image-based media) or written (readable texts). The authors state there is "no one-fitting-all approach to classify them" since many resources mix both kinds of content, and argue institutions can use such profiling to guide investment decisions.
requirements: The resource must require a one-time or continuous financial investment; free platforms such as YouTube channels and textbooks are excluded from the classification
constraints: Many resources provide both content types with one aspect more prominent, so categories are not mutually exclusive
target_learners: medical students (pre-clinical and clinical phases)
examples: The survey classified requested premium resources by method (written 68.9%, visual 95.8%) and by goal (board exam oriented 98.3%, lecture oriented 40.3%)

title: Patient-Provider Interaction Checklist: a 20-item binary scoring instrument for medical interview components in Spanish
description: The Patient-Provider Interaction Checklist is a 20-item binary scoring instrument completed by the course facilitator during a standardized patient encounter. Each item is "awarded 0 points if the student failed to perform the required action, and 1 point if the student made a clear and effective effort to perform the required action." Items correspond to components of the medical interview, from initial greeting through medications/allergies, family history, rapport/empathy, and a respectful ending. constraints: Binary scoring is effective for assessing task completion but, per the authors, lacks the nuance needed to differentiate varying levels of language proficiency

article_title: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and academic performance of medical postgraduates.
citation: Yu Yibo, Tang Qiaomei, Shi Haifei, Chen Ting, Wang Yaping, Hu Hanguang, Yao Ke. (2022). The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and academic performance of medical postgraduates. Frontiers in Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9521680/
title: Pandemic-era disruption of postgraduate medical education as a driver of mild mental health symptoms and academic concerns
description: The article organizes its findings around an implicit framework in which pandemic control measures (lockdowns, online learning, reduced hospital internships) disrupt postgraduate medical education, which in turn shapes mental health and academic performance. It reports that "many courses have been transferred from classroom learning to online learning due to the changes in learning and living environments," that "medical students are unable to communicate effectively with teachers, and there is a lack of internship opportunities for clinical learning in the hospital," and that these changes affected mental health and academic performance. The framework distinguishes mental health outcomes (anxiety, depression via GAD-7 and PHQ-9) from academic outcomes (overall impact, graduation-standard worries, course conversion, practice reduction, tutor communication), and identifies gender and grade level as key moderating factors.
requirements: Assessment instruments covering mental health (GAD-7, PHQ-9) and academic performance items to operationalize the outcomes
constraints: Developed from a single-institution cross-sectional survey during one pandemic period in China; the authors note the sample size was relatively small and influencing factors were limited
target_learners: medical postgraduate students (master's and doctoral)
target_learning_goals: understanding how pandemic disruptions affect mental health and academic performance in clinical postgraduate education
examples: The article links postgraduates' academic concerns to the increase in offline-to-online course conversion, reduced practical operations, and less teacher-student interaction reported in Table 4

citation: Jang Yujin, Suh Youngmeen. (2021). Longitudinal Effects of Parental Academic Support on Academic Achievement in Korea: Will You Be a Companion or a Manager in Your Children’s Academic Support? International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182010823
title: Two types of parental academic support: PAS as a companion and PAS as a manager
description: The article introduces a novel two-dimensional conceptualization of parental academic support (PAS) derived by factor analysis of eight Likert items. PAS as a companion covers "the situation in which parents studied with children, taught children themselves, advised them how to study, and created a learning atmosphere at home"; PAS as a manager covers situations where "parents decided on children’s private tutoring or private educational institutes, spared no money for children’s studies, and managed children’s grades and schedules". The two types correlate highly (r = 0.55) yet show divergent longitudinal effects, so the distinction is meaningful despite shared variance.
requirements: PAS must be measured with enough items to distinguish the two types; the authors note "more items are needed to discern the PAS type"
constraints: The types were extracted from Korean fifth graders' perceptions; the authors caution relationships "might be stronger in Korean children than they would be in Western samples because of sociocultural factors"
target_learners: elementary school students transitioning to adolescence (fifth graders in the KELS panel)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement (Korean, mathematics, English test scores) supported by motivation and self-regulation

title: Parents should support children's studies as companions—learning with them—rather than as managers of schedules and grades
description: The article recommends that parental academic support take the form of companionship: studying with the child, advising, and creating a learning atmosphere, rather than managing grades, schedules, and private education. It concludes that "Parents should not support their children’s studies by acting as a manager of their children’s time and grades but by learning with and accompanying their children", because managerial support raised amotivation while companion support fostered self-regulation and achievement over three years.
requirements: Support must respect the child's autonomy; the article states "it is important when supporting children’s studies to respect their autonomy, and parents and children should be on an equal footing"
constraints: Evidence comes from Korean fifth graders' perceptions in the KELS panel; the authors caution some parent-related relationships "might be stronger in Korean children than they would be in Western samples because of sociocultural factors"
target_learners: children in late childhood and early adolescence
target_learning_goals: academic achievement, self-regulation, and intrinsic motivation
examples: In the KELS panel, children perceiving companion-type support in fifth grade showed higher self-regulation and achievement three years later, while manager-type support predicted higher amotivation

title: Four-typology parenting style classification based on responsiveness and demandingness
description: The article describes parenting style as "a constellation of two underlying dimensions: responsiveness and demandingness". Crossing these two dimensions yields four types: authoritative (responsive and demanding), authoritarian (demanding but not responsive), permissive (responsive but not demanding), and neglectful (neither). The study measured these via the Authoritative Parenting Index and used median splits to categorize adolescents' perceived parenting styles as a covariate in the achievement models.

constraints: Styles were created using median splits on the two dimensions in this sample
target_learners: high school adolescents aged 15-18
examples: In the study sample, 31.4% of adolescents were classified as having authoritative parents, 29.3% authoritarian, 19.9% permissive, and 19.4% neglectful

title: Padova resident CVC training pathway (didactic lessons, simulation center practice, and supervised procedural experience)
description: An institutional training pathway described in the article's Methods: from the first year of residency, residents follow frontal lessons (anatomy, CVC usage and complications), attend operating rooms to become familiar with surgical patients and devices, and participate in simulation courses at an active simulation center (running since 2007) using a variety of skill trainers to develop ultrasound and eye-hand coordination. constraints: Proficiency status is defined case by case by local institutional protocol, usually when last-year residents have performed at least 50 catheterizations, an arbitrary cut-off the authors acknowledge
